decisions.quote: In Husnu and Crisp (2010), British non- Muslim participants were assigned to either imagine interacting with a British Muslim stranger or to imagine that they were walking outdoors (control condition). Participants imagined the scene for one minute, and then described their thoughts for an additional minute before indicating their interest and willingness to interact with British Muslims on a four item scale.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind target 10 identify Study 1 of Husnu and Crisp (2010) as the original study re-tested for the imagined contact effect.

decisions.quote:
A large scale replication with 36 samples successfully replicated eleven of thirteen classic 

and contemporary effects in psychological science, some of which are well-known to be robust, and 

others that have been replicated infrequently or not at all. The original studies produced 

underestimates of some effects (e.g., anchoring-and-adjustment and allowed versus forbidden 

message framing), and overestimates of other effects (e.g., imagined contact producing willingness 

to interact with outgroups in the future). Two effects – flag priming influencing conservatism and 

currency priming influencing system justification – did not replicate.
decisions.reason: The discussion states an overall verdict that eleven of the thirteen effects successfully replicated, explicitly placing imagined contact among the replicated effectswhose original effect size was overestimated, and per the codebook a smaller or weaker supported effect is coded as successful rather than mixed.

decisions.quote: As a possible account for the sex gap in participation in science and math, Nosek and colleagues (2002) found that women had more negative implicit attitudes toward math compared to arts than men did in two studies of Yale undergraduates. Participants completed four Implicit Association Tests (IATs) in random order, one of which measured associations of math and arts with positivity and negativity. The replication simplified the design for length to be just a single IAT.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind target 11 identify Nosek, Banaji, and Greenwald (2002) as the original study re-tested in Effects 12 and 13.

decisions.quote: This research tested variation in the replicability of thirteen classic and contemporary effects across 36 independent samples totaling 6,344 participants.
decisions.reason: The paper collected new data to re-test the flag priming effect from Carter, Ferguson, and Hassin (2011).

decisions.quote: Carter et al. (2011) examined how subtle exposure to the flag may increase conservatism among U.S. participants. Participants were presented with four photos and asked to estimate the time of day at which they were taken. In the flag- prime condition, the American flag appeared in two of these photos. In the control condition, the same photos were presented without flags. Following the manipulation, participants completed an 8-item questionnaire assessing views toward various political issues (e.g., abortion, gun control, affirmative action). Participants in the flag-primed condition indicated significantly more conservative positions than those in the control condition. The priming stimuli used to replicate this finding were obtained from the authors and identical to those used in the original study.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind target 8 identify Carter, Ferguson, and Hassin (2011; Study 2) as the original study re-tested for flag priming.

decisions.quote: And two effects – flag priming influencing conservatism and currency priming influencing system justification – did not replicate.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind coder agree with the authors' explicit verdict that the flag priming effect did not replicate.

decisions.quote:
Oppenheimer et al. 

(2009; adapted from Thaler, 1985) asked participants to imagine that they have tickets to see 

their favorite football team play an important game, but that it is freezing cold on the day of 

the game. Participants rated their likelihood of attending the game on a 9-point scale (1 = 

definitely stay at home, 9 = definitely go to the game). Participants were marginally more 

likely to go to the game if they had paid for the ticket than if the ticket had been free.
decisions.reason: The paper directly re-tests the sunk cost scenario from Oppenheimer, Meyvis, and Davidenko (2009) as Effect 1 of its thirteen replicated effects and reports a successful replication (t = 10.83, p < .001), making this an omitted target.

corrected_value.title: The current status of American public opinion.
corrected_value.authors: Hyman, H. H., & Sheatsley, P. B.

decisions.quote:
In the original study, American participants answered two questions: 

whether communist countries should allow American reporters in and allow them to report 

the news back to American papers and whether America should allow communist reporters 

into the United States and allow them to report back to their papers. Participants reported 

more support for allowing communist reporters into America when that question was asked 

after the question about allowing American reporters into the communist countries.
decisions.reason: The paper re-tests the norm of reciprocity effect from Hyman and Sheatsley (1950) as Effect 6 of the thirteen effects and successfully replicates it (χ2 = 135.3, p < .001), making this an omitted target.

decisions.quote:
Rugg (1941) 

found that respondents were less likely to endorse forbidding speeches against democracy 

than they were to not endorse allowing speeches against democracy. Respondents in the 

United States were asked, in one condition, if the U.S. should allow speeches against 

democracy or, in another condition, whether the U.S. should forbid speeches against 

democracy. 62 percent of participants indicated “No” when asked if speeches against 

democracy should be allowed, but only 46 percent indicated “Yes” when asked if these 

speeches should be forbidden. In the replication, the words “The United States” were 

replaced with the name of the country the study was administered in.
decisions.reason: The paper re-tests Rugg (1941) on allowed versus forbidden question wording as Effect 7 of the thirteen effects and explicitly notes its successful replication (χ2 = 3088.7, p < .001), making this an omitted target.

decisions.quote: Lorge and Curtis (1936) examined how an identical quote would be perceived if it was attributed to a liked or disliked individual. Participants were asked to rate their agreement with a list of quotations. The quotation of interest was, “I hold it that a little rebellion, now and then, is a good thing, and as necessary in the political world as storms are in the physical world.” In one condition the quote was attributed to Thomas Jefferson, a liked individual, and in the other it was attributed to Vladimir Lenin, a disliked individual. More agreement was observed when the quote was attributed to Jefferson than Lenin (reported in Moskowitz, 2004).
decisions.reason: The paper re-tests the quote attribution effect of Lorge and Curtis (1936) as Effect 8 of the thirteen effects and successfully replicates it (t = 12.79, p < .001), making this an omitted target.
